questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the literal meaning of nánshòu?
How do you make it clear you mean sadness, not physical pain?
How does Chinese differ from English in "eating it up"?
Name the three main uses of nòng.
Write the Chinese for "I'm too full, I can't eat any more."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ chīde tài bǎo le, chībuxiàqu le.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Don't fool with my watch."
Give three verbs formed with nòng plus a result.

answers.answer_text: Any three of: nòngzāng ("to make dirty"), nòngpò ("to break"), nòngsǐ ("to kill"), nònghuài ("to break"), nòngqīngchu ("to get clear").

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Where did you get this from?"

answers.answer_text: Yes — it can be used for physical aches and pains or emotional ones.

articles.text:
2. A: Nǐ zěnme bù chī le?           Why aren't you eating?
   B: Wǒde wèi hěn nánshòu,         My stomach is uncomfortable, I can't
      chībuxiàqu le.                 eat anymore.
   A: Nà wǒ qù gěi ni nòng diǎnr    I'll go get you some soup then.
      tāng lai.

Notes on No. 2

nánshòu: "to feel uncomfortable; to feel bad, to feel unhappy," literally "to find something hard to bear." This adjectival verb can be used for PHYSICAL aches and pains, or EMOTIONAL ones.

Zhēn ràng rén nánshòu.           It really makes one feel bad.

To make it clear you are talking about SADNESS and not a physical pain, use the phrase xīnli hěn nánshòu.

chībuxiàqu: "unable to eat (it all) up." Here -xiàqu is used for its meaning as a DIRECTIONAL ending. While in English we might say "eat it UP," the Chinese say "eat it DOWN." Using hē, "to drink," you can also say hēxiàqu.

chīdexiàqu    able to eat it down
chībuxiàqu    unable to eat it down
méi chīxiaqu  didn't eat it down
chīxiaqu le   ate it down

Wǒ chīde tài bǎo le, chībuxiàqu  I'm too full, I can't eat any more.
le.
Zhèige yào chīxiaqu jiù huì hǎo  You'll feel better after you take
le.                              this medicine.

nòng: This is a VERY COMMON verb with several especially useful meanings.

(1) "to do, to make" in a broad, vague sense:
Zánmen kāishǐ nòng fàn, hǎo bu   Let's start to make dinner, okay?
hǎo?
Tā bù zhīdào zěnme nòngle        Somehow he made himself a lot of
hǎoduō qián.                     money.

(2) "to play with, to fool with, to monkey with":
Bié nòng wǒde biǎo.              Don't fool with my watch.

(3) Nòng can be FOLLOWED BY ANOTHER VERB showing the result: nòngzāng, "to make dirty"; nòngpò, "to break"; nòngsǐ, "to kill."

Shì shéi bǎ wǒde yǔsǎn nònghuài  Who was it who broke my umbrella?
le?
Zhèige wèntí hěn yàojǐn, děi     This question is very important, we
nòngqīngchu.                     must get it clear.
Nǐ nòngcuò le ba, tā qùnián cái  You're mistaken, I think. He didn't
cóng dàlù chūlai.                leave the mainland until last year.

nònglai: "to get and bring (here)."

Nǐ cóng nǎr nònglaide?           Where did you get this from?
